title: Model Evaluation and Validation
summary: Choosing and interpreting the right evaluation strategy separates a reliable model from a misleading one. Different problems demand different metrics, and validation techniques ensure your performance estimates generalize. Learning curves reveal whet
content:
# Model Evaluation and Validation ##### Two curves that told the whole story A team spent three weeks trying to improve a model stuck at 71% validation accuracy. They tried gradient boosting, then a neural network, then extensive hyperparameter tuning. Nothing moved. Then someone plotted a **learning curve** — training and validation score against the number of training samples. Both curves were flat, close together, and low. Training accuracy was 73%; validation was 71%. That shape has an unambiguous diagnosis: **high bias**. The model was not overfitting — the gap was tiny. It was underfitting, and more data or more model capacity of the same kind would not help. The features simply did not contain enough information about the target. They went back to feature engineering, added three domain-derived ratios and a temporal aggregate, and reached 84% in two days. Three weeks of tuning versus five minutes of plotting. **Evaluation is not the step after modelling — it is the step that tells you what to do next.** ##### Classification metrics in depth Yesterday's material introduced precision, recall and F1. The depth worth adding is about which metric answers which question, and where each misleads. ```python from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, fbeta_score, roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, matthews_corrcoef, balanced_accuracy_score, log_loss) y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] y_pred = (y_prob >= 0.5).astype(int) print(f"Accuracy {accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred):.3f}") print(f"Balanced accuracy {balanced_accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred):.3f}") print(f"Precision {precision_score(y_test, y_pred):.3f}") print(f"Recall {recall_score(y_test, y_pred):.3f}") print(f"F1 {f1_score(y_test, y_pred):.3f}") print(f"F2 (recall-heavy) {fbeta_score(y_test, y_pred, beta=2):.3f}") print(f"MCC {matthews_corrcoef(y_test, y_pred):.3f}") print(f"ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob):.3f}") print(f"PR-AUC {average_precision_score(y_test, y_prob):.3f}") print(f"Log loss {log_loss(y_test, y_prob):.3f}") ``` Three of these deserve more attention than they usually get. **F-beta** generalizes F1 by weighting recall relative to precision. `beta=2` weights recall twice as heavily; `beta=0.5` favours precision. When you know the cost asymmetry — a missed fraud costs ₹40,000, a false alarm costs ₹200 of review time — F-beta encodes it directly rather than forcing you to argue about F1. **Matthews Correlation Coefficient** ranges from −1 to +1 and uses all four confusion-matrix cells. It is the most honest single number on imbalanced data: the always-predict-negative model that scored 99.2% accuracy in yesterday's mammogram story scores **MCC = 0**, because MCC only rewards genuine correlation between prediction and truth. **Log loss** measures probability quality rather than classification correctness. A model predicting 0.51 for a positive and one predicting 0.99 both get it "right," but log loss distinguishes them. Use it when the probability itself drives a downstream decision — expected-value calculations, risk pricing, ranking. **Calibration** is the related concern. A well-calibrated model that says "70% likely" should be right about 70% of the time: ```python from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve, CalibratedClassifierCV prob_true, prob_pred = calibration_curve(y_test, y_prob, n_bins=10) # Plot prob_pred vs prob_true — perfect calibration is the diagonal calibrated = CalibratedClassifierCV(model, method="isotonic", cv=5) ``` Random Forests and SVMs are typically poorly calibrated — forests push probabilities toward the middle, SVMs toward the extremes. If you use the probability as a number rather than just thresholding it, calibrate. ##### Regression metrics in depth ```python from sklearn.metrics import (mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score, mean_absolute_percentage_error, median_absolute_error) mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred) rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred)) medae = median_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred) mape = mean_absolute_percentage_error(y_test, y_pred) print(f"MAE {mae:>12,.0f} RMSE {rmse:>12,.0f} ratio {rmse/mae:.2f}") print(f"MedAE {medae:>12,.0f} MAPE {mape:>12.1%}") ``` The **RMSE/MAE ratio** is a diagnostic worth knowing. For normally distributed errors it is around 1.25. A ratio of 2 or more means a few very large errors are dominating — you have outliers, and you should look at the worst predictions individually rather than only at the aggregate. **MAPE** expresses error as a percentage, which stakeholders understand instantly, but it breaks when actual values approach zero (division blows up) and it penalizes over-prediction more than under-prediction. **Median absolute error** is the outlier-robust alternative to MAE. Beyond metrics, always inspect the **error distribution**: ```python residuals = y_test - y_pred print(f"Mean residual: {residuals.mean():>10,.0f}") # should be ≈ 0 print(f"Worst 5 errors:\n{pd.Series(np.abs(residuals)).nlargest(5)}") ``` A non-zero mean residual means systematic bias — the model consistently over- or under-predicts, which no single accuracy metric reveals. ##### Learning curves A **learning curve** plots performance against training set size. It answers the question that determines your next move: *would more data help?* ```python from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve import matplotlib.pyplot as plt train_sizes, train_scores, val_scores = learning_curve( model, X, y, cv=5, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1, train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10), ) train_mean, train_std = train_scores.mean(axis=1), train_scores.std(axis=1) val_mean, val_std = val_scores.mean(axis=1), val_scores.std(axis=1) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5)) ax.plot(train_sizes, train_mean, "o-", label="Training") ax.fill_between(train_sizes, train_mean - train_std, train_mean + train_std, alpha=0.15) ax.plot(train_sizes, val_mean, "s-", label="Validation") ax.fill_between(train_sizes, val_mean - val_std, val_mean + val_std, alpha=0.15) ax.set_xlabel("Training samples"); ax.set_ylabel("F1"); ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3) ``` Three shapes, three diagnoses: | Shape | Diagnosis | What to do | |---|---|---| | Both curves low, converged, small gap | **High bias / underfitting** | Better features, more model capacity, less regularization | | Training high, validation much lower, gap not closing | **High variance / overfitting** | More data, regularization, simpler model, feature selection | | Both high and converged | Good fit | Ship it — or improve features for further gains | | Validation still rising at maximum data | Data-limited | **More data will help** — collect it | That last row is genuinely valuable: it is the only reliable way to know whether collecting more data is worth the expense. If the validation curve has plateaued, more of the same data will not help. **Validation curves** answer a different question — how does one hyperparameter affect the fit? ```python from sklearn.model_selection import validation_curve depths = [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 30, None] train_s, val_s = validation_curve( DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42), X, y, param_name="max_depth", param_range=depths, cv=5, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1, ) ``` Plot both curves against depth and you get the classic figure: training score rising monotonically while validation rises, peaks, and declines. The peak is your optimal complexity, and the widening gap beyond it is overfitting made visible. ##### Cross-validation strategies The mechanics were covered yesterday; the emphasis here is on **matching the strategy to the failure mode you are trying to avoid**. ```python from sklearn.model_selection import (StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit, RepeatedStratifiedKFold, cross_validate) # Classification with imbalance — preserve class ratios in every fold cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) # Small dataset — repeat with different shuffles to reduce estimate variance cv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3, random_state=42) # Repeated entities — no customer in both train and validation cv = GroupKFold(n_splits=5) scores = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv, groups=customer_ids, scoring="f1") # Temporal — never train on the future cv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=7) # gap avoids leakage at the boundary ``` That `gap` parameter is a detail worth knowing: if your features include a 7-day rolling average, the last week of the training fold overlaps informationally with the start of the validation fold. A gap removes it. **Nested cross-validation** is the rigorous approach when you both tune and evaluate. An inner loop selects hyperparameters; an outer loop estimates performance. Without it, the score you report is optimistic because hyperparameters were chosen using the same folds you evaluated on: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, cross_val_score inner = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=42) outer = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) search = GridSearchCV(model, param_grid, cv=inner, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1) nested_scores = cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=outer, scoring="f1") print(f"Unbiased estimate: {nested_scores.mean():.3f} ± {nested_scores.std():.3f}") ``` It costs `inner × outer` fits, so use it when the honesty of the number matters — reporting results, comparing to a published baseline, or deciding whether to deploy. ##### Handling class imbalance Three levers, and the important point is **where in the pipeline each belongs**. ```python from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE from imblearn.under_sampling import RandomUnderSampler from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline # 1. Class weights — no data manipulation, works with most estimators model = RandomForestClassifier(class_weight="balanced", random_state=42) # 2. Resampling — MUST be inside the pipeline so it applies per-fold pipeline = ImbPipeline([ ("prep", preprocessor), ("smote", SMOTE(random_state=42, k_neighbors=5)), ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)), ]) # 3. Combined over- and under-sampling pipeline = ImbPipeline([ ("over", SMOTE(sampling_strategy=0.3, random_state=42)), # minority to 30% ("under", RandomUnderSampler(sampling_strategy=0.6, random_state=42)), ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)), ]) ``` SMOTE (Chawla et al., 2002) synthesizes new minority examples by interpolating between a point and its nearest minority neighbours, rather than duplicating existing rows — which reduces the overfitting that naive oversampling causes. **The critical rule: resampling belongs inside the cross-validation loop, never before it.** Using `imblearn`'s Pipeline guarantees this; SMOTE applied to the whole dataset before splitting creates synthetic points derived from validation samples, and the resulting scores can be inflated by ten points or more. Often the simplest lever is best: **train normally and tune the threshold**: ```python from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_test, y_prob) # Find the threshold achieving at least 80% recall, maximizing precision viable = recall[:-1] >= 0.80 best_idx = np.argmax(precision[:-1] * viable) print(f"Threshold {thresholds[best_idx]:.3f} → " f"precision {precision[best_idx]:.3f}, recall {recall[best_idx]:.3f}") ``` This costs nothing, requires no synthetic data, and directly encodes a business requirement ("we must catch 80% of fraud"). ##### Model interpretation A model you cannot explain is difficult to trust, debug or defend. ```python from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance, PartialDependenceDisplay # Permutation importance — shuffle a feature, measure the performance drop. # More reliable than tree feature_importances_, which is biased toward # high-cardinality features. result = permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=10, random_state=42, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1) importances = pd.Series(result.importances_mean, index=X_test.columns) print(importances.nlargest(10).round(4)) # Partial dependence — how does the prediction change as one feature varies? PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(model, X_test, features=["tenure_months", "age"]) ``` For per-prediction explanations, **SHAP** decomposes an individual prediction into contributions from each feature — indispensable when someone asks "why was *this* application rejected?" A caution: permutation importance on correlated features understates both, because shuffling one leaves its correlated partner to carry the signal. Group correlated features or interpret with that in mind. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Trained model] --> B[Plot learning curve] B --> C{Shape?} C -->|both low, small gap| D[HIGH BIAS
better features, more capacity,
less regularization] C -->|big gap, train high| E[HIGH VARIANCE
more data, regularize,
simplify, feature selection] C -->|val still rising| F[DATA-LIMITED
collect more] C -->|both high, converged| G[Good fit] D --> H[Validation curve
per hyperparameter] E --> H G --> I[Choose metric by cost
F-beta / MCC / PR-AUC] I --> J[Tune threshold on
the PR curve] J --> K[Interpret: permutation
importance + PDP + SHAP] K --> L[Report with CV spread
+ error analysis] ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Not plotting learning curves** — three weeks of tuning that five minutes would have redirected. - **Accuracy on imbalanced data**; use MCC, balanced accuracy or PR-AUC. - **SMOTE before splitting**, leaking synthetic validation data into training. - **Tuning and evaluating on the same folds** without nesting, producing optimistic scores. - **Reporting a mean without a standard deviation.** - **Assuming probabilities are calibrated** when using them as numbers. - **Tree `feature_importances_`** as ground truth — it is biased toward high-cardinality features. - **Ignoring the RMSE/MAE ratio** and missing outlier-dominated error. - **No error analysis** — the worst predictions usually share a pattern that points at a fix. - **Optimizing a metric nobody chose deliberately**, rather than one derived from the cost of each error type. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **plot learning curves to diagnose overfitting versus underfitting**, and **apply a technique to handle a class-imbalanced dataset**. Produce all three curve shapes deliberately — an over-regularized model, an unconstrained one, and a well-tuned one — so you learn to recognize the shapes rather than merely read about them. The mini project is an **evaluation report generator**: given a trained model and dataset, output all relevant metrics, curves, and a **plain-language diagnosis**. The diagnosis is the interesting engineering. Encode the rules from the table above — "training F1 0.98, validation F1 0.71, gap 0.27: the model is overfitting; consider regularization, more training data, or feature selection." A tool that interprets its own output is far more useful than one that prints numbers, and it forces you to make your diagnostic reasoning explicit. For the assignment, **diagnose a learning curve showing high training accuracy and low validation accuracy, and propose three fixes**. The diagnosis is overfitting / high variance. Strong fixes, in order of expected impact: more training data (the validation curve's slope tells you whether this will help); regularization or reduced model complexity — lower `max_depth`, higher `alpha`, dropout; and feature selection or dimensionality reduction to cut the noise the model is fitting. Explain *why* each addresses variance specifically, because that reasoning is what the question is testing. ##### Key takeaways - Learning curves diagnose whether you have a bias problem, a variance problem, or a data-quantity problem — plot them before tuning anything. - Choose metrics from the cost of each error type: F-beta encodes asymmetry, MCC is honest on imbalanced data, log loss and calibration matter when probabilities drive decisions. - Match the cross-validation strategy to the leakage risk — stratified, grouped, or time-series with a gap — and use nested CV when the reported number must be unbiased. - Resampling belongs inside the pipeline so it applies per-fold; threshold tuning is often simpler and encodes business requirements directly. - Interpret with permutation importance and partial dependence rather than raw tree importances, and always do error analysis on the worst predictions.
